headline: Subscription pricing, trials & billing is the single largest fixable drag on the rating.

themes.theme: Subscription pricing and free trial structure
themes.summary: Many customers object to the pricing model—finding subscriptions expensive, mandatory, or deceptive—while others find the value reasonable; significant frustration over hidden trial conditions, aggressive billing practices, and the mismatch between advertised 'free' offerings and required payment methods.
themes.action: Redesign the trial experience: offer a genuinely free tier with basic features (e.g., 5–10 hours/month, 1–2 voices) before requiring payment, or implement a 'try first, pay later' onboarding that does not request payment info until after the trial ends.

themes.summary: Users struggle to cancel subscriptions, change payment methods, or receive customer support; some are charged unexpectedly after trial periods or encounter account verification issues that block access despite active payments.
themes.action: Simplify subscription cancellation by adding a one-click cancel option in the app settings; implement transparent email reminders before billing; establish a responsive human support channel accessible via in-app chat or email.

themes.theme: App crashes, bugs, and technical stability
themes.summary: Users report frequent app crashes, freezes, playback failures, buffering issues, offline download problems, and performance degradation over time, which undermine the experience even for paying subscribers.
themes.action: Conduct a comprehensive code audit and performance review; implement automated crash reporting in the app; establish a public bug tracker so users can report and track resolution of issues in real time.

themes.theme: Listening hours limits and offline download restrictions
themes.summary: Free and paid tiers offer limited listening hours (10/month free, 24/month on some plans) and hidden or unexplained offline download limits, forcing users to pay for additional hours mid-listen or preventing offline access despite paid subscriptions.
themes.action: Clarify and publish all usage limits upfront (listening hours, offline downloads, voice count) before checkout; consider offering unlimited hours for premium subscribers or raising the free tier hours and communicating the reason for limits.

themes.summary: The app struggles with punctuation, citations, formatting (e.g., line breaks, headers, in-text numbers), non-English pronunciation (pinyin, accented words), and contextual understanding, which can distort meaning and disrupt listening experience.
themes.action: Build or improve the text pre-processing pipeline to handle punctuation, citations, headers, and special characters correctly; add language-specific rules for non-English pronunciation; allow users to configure which elements to skip (e.g., footnote citations).

themes.summary: Users find the app interface unintuitive, with frequent layout changes between updates that move or hide frequently-used features (content menu, chapter summary, pause controls), causing frustration and rework of muscle memory.
themes.action: Establish a stable UI layout and communicate any planned changes in advance; allow user customization of button placement and prominent controls; conduct usability testing before major UI updates.

themes.summary: Customers appreciate the ability to upload personal files (EPUB, PDF, Kindle, Google Docs, web articles) and have them read aloud, but some struggle with import functionality, limited content in the native library, and difficulty connecting services like Kindle.
themes.action: Improve the Kindle import workflow with step-by-step guidance and error messages; expand native audiobook library partnerships; provide in-app tutorials for importing from different sources.

themes.summary: Customers consistently praise the natural, human-like quality of the AI voices and the diversity of voice options available, though some report occasional glitches, pronunciation issues, and inconsistent performance across different voices.
themes.action: Establish a voice quality assurance process to catch and fix pronunciation errors, extended vowel sounds, and glitches before release; create a feedback loop for users to report voice issues by specific voice ID.

themes.summary: Customers express strong satisfaction with the app's core value—transforming text into natural-sounding audio that enables multitasking, supports accessibility, and enhances learning—though technical and pricing issues temper enthusiasm for some.
themes.action: Leverage positive sentiment by creating a structured feedback program for feature requests; highlight accessibility and learning use cases in marketing; develop case studies with dyslexic users and ADHD communities to demonstrate impact.

reviews.author: JeffyMakesItFun
reviews.text:
ElevenReader is what happens when text-to-speech stops sounding like a GPS having an existential crisis.

The killer feature for me is being able to toss in an EPUB, PDF, article, or other reading material and basically manufacture my own audiobook. The voice selection is wildly good—natural enough that I can actually disappear into a story instead of constantly noticing that I’m listening to AI.

I especially love having control over the narrator. Sometimes a perfectly good audiobook gets absolutely murdered by a voice that doesn’t fit the characters, and ElevenReader basically says, “Okay babe, pick another one.”

It’s also fantastic for turning things I need to read into things I can listen to while driving, cleaning, or wandering around pretending I have my life together.

This app has legitimately increased how much I read. That’s the whole ballgame.

reviews.author: Uptown, Chicago
reviews.text:
I am like an actor who can’t watch themselves act on camera, which makes it very difficult for me to edit. This helps not only with this, but with fiction, hearing what a story sounds like if the character’s a man versus a woman, if they all sound alike. You can be fooled into thinking your writing sounds better than it is. I get caught up in a whimsical wordplay that are a lot of alliteration that might work on the page but doesn’t sound right, or sounds beautiful but looks weird. 

Invaluable tool that raised me from a kid who never got a single A in school, to using this to help me read back my notes from class, class assignments, it helps me hear what a psycho I sound like when I text a paragraph sometimes, there’s times people open up to me and it’s too much for me to read, so I’ll copy it into here and have it read like a romcom letter being read in an 80/90s movie nostalgia. 

It’s not something you really know how much and what a wide range of things you can use it for. If I’m writing out something angry snit something, I can hear it, and it lets you bookmark the moment so you can continue forward without getting hung, like I often do when reading, reading the same page over and over.  to put it much more efficiently. 

There’s just too much to read to be an A student. And for me, I love reading, this makes me read books more because there’s such a free flow thought process triggered by a recollective memory. 

The rhythm requires phonic spelling sometimes if you want to get real in the weeds with it, but for the most part, finding the voice of the character is just a cool manifestation that prior to only the luckiest few ever got to see their words played out. This is technology at its best. No better app. I’m a broke 32 year old going back to school after a seven year stint in the hospital recovering from an SCI that left me paralyzed. I dedicated my life to walking and writing. But the pain I was in, all the time, made reading difficult to fight through or find the storied rhythm because I was always shifting in pain. I couldn’t take anything for the pain when I read either because then I didn’t retain or follow anything. 

This app changed that for me. No more excuses. For essays, or news articles, investigative reporting pieces for creative nonfiction or brainstorming, this is perfect for. 

I have a Freewrite, before I do anything, the first thing I do is upload it as is into here. I print it off and listen to it, I try to listen to it all the way through at least once when editing because a lot of times the questions raised or the phrasing it should be, is there, you just forgot. I forget honestly most of what I write when I write fiction or creative nonfiction. I’m so insecure about my writing, my body will go blank with words stuck unreadable on the page… but the fact that this reads through whatever the bottleneck you’re stuck on, plays a huge role on my new trend of actually finishing all my pieces of work I start. Obviously the deadlines of school play large part in that. 

The academic texts are some of the more laborious reads in the world for some. Not for me. Not when it’s Maya Angelou or James Dean, or some satirical southern voice. Hearing such a range of voices has given my characters a much more colorful charisma, much because I can typewrite infinitely on an electronics-ink scroll, and truly find the heart of the character. 99% of it is never used, but take away the names, you can still tell who’s talking in my writing, I thank the app for. 

It’s the procrastination meet between. I get frozen. Literally frozen. Fight or flight or freeze. This plays whether my brain and body want to participate or not. And it’s just such a learning tool, not at all to replace reading, but breaking through and getting the most out of reading which in return gets the most out of you. 

I don’t always have the money each month, but easy cancel, easy to sign back up. Definitely worth the money, but truly good to the customers, even the free ones. I don’t know how long that lasts, but whenever I have projects due, or a story idea hits me, a text becomes an email, an email becomes a movie idea, a movie idea becomes a neat idea but when you listen back to you can hear the holes and what it lacks beyond the idea to make to make it a full story.  Paying for it is mandatory when I’m doing so much research pulling an all nighter, spending all my efforts into the writing, too tired to read it over carefully (too subjectively close to it as well). This helps monumentally by showing you to hear your words from another. 

I use this the most before sending any well written emails. I get the satisfaction of hearing it said, but save myself the embarrassment of having sent it, let alone sent it with that many spelling errors you could hear but speech didn’t pick up. I tend to do several drafts, often quite differently at first to see the direction the story takes me.. or combing through the tons and tons of research and original documents, allowing you to stretch your eyes and walk around. I put in all my notes, read my handwritten ones or take a picture of them, have Claude transcribe them as is, errors and all, put it in. And listen to it broken. Sometimes those errors can be harmonic and when you hear it, it Vicks, saying it out loud. All teachers tell us to read our work out loud. But online in a studio apartment and the way I read it is so vastly different than how a normal objective reader would. There’s a time to read aloud and there’s a time to listen.  

I put all my notes I write from class into Claude, have it organized specifically to optimize the sound of the words aspect of this app. Because  I need to hear it read back to me so I know what I said verbatim, and monitor when and if my writing’s language has been changed in any way without my permission or direction, which happens, but come finals, or when during the all nighters, this is it. The best app I’ve ever used.

But online in a studio apartment and the way I read it is so vastly different than how a normal objective reader would.
There’s a time to read aloud and there’s a time to listen.
I put all my notes I write from class into Claude, have it organized specifically to optimize the sound of the words aspect of this app.

Because I need to hear it read back to me so I know what I said verbatim, and monitor when and if my writing’s language has been changed in any way without my permission or direction, which happens, but come finals, or when during the all nighters, this is it.
The best app I’ve ever used.

summary.headline: Subscription pricing, trials & billing is the single largest fixable drag on the rating.
key_findings: Subscription flow is the top-volume negative driver: 48 reviews, -0.416★ rating impact, flagged 'Fix first'.
App stability compounds the damage: 35 reviews, -0.354 sentiment, -0.284★ impact, large effect, also 'Fix first'.
Overall app experience and voice quality are the assets to protect: +0.835★ impact on 56 reviews and +0.197★ on 25 reviews, both large positive effects.
Small-volume issues carry outsized pain: Customer support (8 reviews, -0.597 sentiment) and Account signup (9 reviews, -0.5 sentiment, concentrated on Google Play) are both flagged 'Investigate'.
